issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. 'Specific body parts associated with the event,' 'power imbalance,' and 'being alone with women' are much more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual assault formulations than toxic exposure.

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items point to incompatible trauma meanings: body-part cues, gendered interpersonal cues, and power-over-me situations imply an assaultive perpetrator context rather than an occupational chemical exposure event.

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male bomb disposal technician whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It implies an interpersonal/sexual-threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the threat items, which instead reflect generalized physical danger/hypervigilance.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure, which typically does not involve an identifiable perpetrator. This item suggests an assault/interpersonal trauma formulation and is inconsistent with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new relationships is hard to reconcile with a 62-year-old married bomb disposal technician whose indexed trauma is toxic chemical exposure; this strategy fits interpersonal trauma or betrayal formulations more than exposure-related PTSD, and there are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items to support an interpersonal-relationship focus.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone in a room or building does not connect well to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe generalized hypervigilance and escape planning, while the trauma type and other selected triggers do not suggest solitary settings as a specific danger cue. This looks like a maladaptive strategy for a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is difficult to integrate with toxic chemical exposure and the rest of the selected profile. The other triggers are workplace and loud noises, and the threat items reflect environmental danger monitoring rather than coercion or dominance. This trigger suggests an interpersonal/control-based trauma theme that is unsupported elsewhere.

vignette: Kwame had spent thirty-eight years in the high-bay chemical disposal facility, but the day the pressurized solvent tank ruptured still played out behind his eyes with startling clarity. He was recalibrating the extraction arm when a hydraulic valve blew with a sharp, concussive crack that shook the concrete floor. A white plume of toxic mist rolled through the aisle, stinging his eyes and burning his throat. He remembered gripping the metal railing, his palms slick with sweat, as the emergency alarms shrieked and the heavy blast doors hissed shut, sealing him in the swirling cloud until the ventilation system finally cleared the air. The treatment began immediately at the on-site clinic, where the sharp tang of antiseptic wipes and the crisp paper of the examination table became deeply woven into his recovery. In the months that followed, the clinic’s antiseptic smell followed him into everyday life. A whiff of cleaning solution in the grocery aisle or the faint chemical bite of his wife’s laundry detergent would make his chest tighten, pulling him back to that sealed aisle and the burning air. Back at the workplace, the routine hum of the ventilation fans and the sudden clatter of a dropped wrench triggered the same tightness. He found himself constantly scanning the high-ceilinged bay, his eyes tracking the overhead pipes, the safety placards, and the positions of the exit doors. He had come to believe that comfort arrived only when he could map every possible way out. When his wife or a colleague approached from behind and laid a hand on his shoulder, he would flinch, his shoulders rising toward his ears before he realized it was only a familiar gesture. The startle did not fade; it simply became a routine part of his day, as constant as the shift whistle. His scanning for danger and his habit of tracing escape routes unfolded side by side, each occupying his attention in the bay and beyond, without one leading to the other. Kwame avoided being alone in rooms or buildings. His avoidance and his overwork developed as parallel habits, each occupying his days. He lingered in the facility’s lobby or walked the perimeter of the loading dock long after his shift ended. He began taking on extra maintenance rounds and staying late to calibrate the decompression chambers. His wife noticed how he packed the guest room with boxes over the years, leaving the master bedroom feeling less like a shared space and more like a place he merely passed through. He also postponed routine physical examinations, steering clear of hospitals and ambulances unless absolutely necessary, wary of the bright lights, the clinical smells, and the sudden proximity of medical staff. His check-ups became careful negotiations, scheduled around his own terms and kept to a minimum. Avoidance of medical cues and his habit of staying late in the workplace ran through his life as separate, steady currents. At sixty-two, Kwame’s work had slowed to a steady, deliberate pace, yet the old vigilance remained. He still mapped the exit routes in every new room, still flinched when a heavy door slammed, still found himself breathing through his mouth when the facility’s solvent drums were moved. The accumulation of these quiet habits had finally drawn him to seek help. His wife had gently placed his PCL-5 score of 57 on the kitchen table, noting how his nights had grown shorter and how he sometimes stood by the bedroom window long after she fell asleep, watching the streetlights and the distant highway. He was uncertain about what lay ahead, unsure whether the world would ever feel truly breathable again, but he had come to the clinic hoping to find a way to live without constantly bracing for the next sharp sound, the next sudden breath of chemical air, or the next unexpected touch.
